## Background

Diabetes mellitus remains a major global public health crisis with a growing burden across adult populations. The etiology of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) involves a complex interplay between modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Excess body weight and body mass index (BMI) is a primary driver of systemic insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic derangement (Yan et al., 2023).

Advancing age is currently beeing studied as a possible independent risk factor for the development of the disease. Characterized by progressive declines in pancreatic $\beta$-cell function, loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia), and reduced peripheral glucose clearance (Malandrino et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2023).

## Aim

This study aims to evaluate the interrelations between age and BMI in the development of diabetes, specifically testing for additive or multiplicative synergistic effects between both variables while investigating sex-specific risk trajectories.

To address these objectives, the study focuses on the following research questions:

1.  **Synergistic Effects:** Is there a statistically significant interaction (additive or multiplicative) between age and BMI in predicting incident diabetes, indicating a synergistic effect between adiposity and advancing age?

2.  **Sexual Dimorphism:** How does the joint impact of age and BMI manifest across biological sexes, and do males and females exhibit distinct risk trajectories over time?

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(here)
library("ggrepel")
```

## Loading data:

```{r}
target_url <- "https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/diabetes.csv"
raw_data_file <- here("data/raw_data/diabetes.csv")

if (file.exists(raw_data_file)){
  diabetes_raw <- read_csv(raw_data_file)
} else {
  diabetes_raw <- read_csv(file = target_url)
  dir.create(path = dirname(raw_data_file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  write_csv(x = diabetes_data, file = raw_data_file)
}
```

## Data Preparation

Before performing PCA, the available variables and their data types were inspected to identify suitable numerical variables for the analysis.

```{r}
names(diabetes_raw)
```

```{r}
glimpse(diabetes_raw)
```

## Data Analysis

### Search for synergetic effects:

We will first represent the data using boxplots to observe general trends. To do that we must first stratify our population based on age and BMI

```{r}

diabetes <- diabetes_raw

BMI_levels <- c("Underweight","Regular wheight", "overwheight","obese")
age_levels <- c("young","adult","mature","old")

# stratifying data
diabetes <- diabetes |> 
  filter(!(is.na(height))) |> 
  filter(!(is.na(weight))) |> 
  mutate(BMI = (weight/(height^2)) * 703) |> 
  mutate(BMI_class = case_when(
    BMI < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
    BMI >= 18.5 & BMI < 25.5 ~ "Regular wheight",
    BMI >= 25.5 & BMI < 30 ~ "overwheight", 
    BMI >= 30 ~ "obese"
  )) |> 
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age < 25 ~ "young",
    age >= 25 & age < 50 ~ "adult",
    age >= 50 & age< 75 ~ "mature", 
    age >= 75 ~ "old"
  ))

# Number of each group:
groups <- diabetes |> 
  group_by(age_group, BMI_class) |> 
  summarize(sum_individuals = n())

total <-  sum(groups$sum_individuals)

groups <- groups |> 
  mutate(prop = sum_individuals/total)

diabetes <- ungroup(diabetes)

BMI_factor <- factor(diabetes$BMI_class, levels = BMI_levels)
age_factor <- factor(age_levels, levels = age_levels)



```

Now we can represent the data:

```{r}

groups_prop <- groups |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  mutate(
    prop = sum_individuals / sum(sum_individuals),
    age_group = paste(
      str_to_sentence(age_group),
      case_match(
        age_group,
        "young" ~ "(<25)",
        "adult" ~ "(25-50)",
        "mature" ~ "(50-75)",
        "old" ~ "(≥75)"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(groups_prop, aes(x = "", y = prop, fill = BMI_class)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ age_group) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Normalized distribution of BMI indexes based on age groups",
    subtitle = "Age ranges (in years) shown in parentheses",
    fill = "BMI Class"
  ) 
```

### Search for sexual dimorphism

To investigate the second research question, we tested whether the way age and BMI relate to diabetes differs between males and females.

Diabetes was defined as glycosylated hemoglobin (`glyhb`) $\geq$ 6.5%

```{r}
diabetes_sex <- diabetes |>
  filter(!is.na(glyhb), !is.na(gender)) |>
  mutate(diabetic = as.integer(glyhb >= 6.5))

# Number of individuals and prevalence by sex
diabetes_sex |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarize(n = n(), prevalence = mean(diabetic))
```

```{r}
ggplot(diabetes_sex, aes(x = age, y = diabetic, colour = BMI_class)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ gender) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of diabetes by age, BMI class and sex",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Probability of diabetes",
    colour = "BMI class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

To test for differences between sexes, we fitted two logistic regression models: one without sex and one where sex interacts with age, BMI and their interaction. Comparing them with a likelihood ratio test tells us whether sex changes the effect of age and BMI.

```{r}
model_no_sex <- glm(diabetic ~ age * BMI, data = diabetes_sex, family = binomial)
model_sex <- glm(diabetic ~ age * BMI * gender, data = diabetes_sex, family = binomial)

anova(model_no_sex, model_sex, test = "Chisq")
```

Finally, the age × BMI model was fitted separately in females and males to compare the effects within each sex.

```{r}
model_female <- glm(diabetic ~ age * BMI,
                    data = filter(diabetes_sex, gender == "female"),
                    family = binomial)

model_male <- glm(diabetic ~ age * BMI,
                  data = filter(diabetes_sex, gender == "male"),
                  family = binomial)

tidy(model_female)
tidy(model_male)
```

### Principal Component Analysis

```{r}
pca_data <- diabetes |>
  select(
    gender,
    BMI_class,
    age,
    BMI,
    waist,
    hip,
    chol,
    stab.glu,
    hdl,
    glyhb,
    bp.1s,
    bp.1d
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```

```{r}
pca_fit <- pca_data |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  prcomp(
    scale = TRUE
  )
pca_scores <- pca_fit |>
  augment(pca_data)

pca_scores |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = .fittedPC1,
      y = .fittedPC2,
      colour = BMI_class,
      shape = gender
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Individuals in PCA Space",
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2",
    colour = "BMI class",
    shape = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
pca_loadings <- pca_fit |>
  tidy(
    matrix = "rotation"
  )

pca_loadings
```

```{r}
arrow_style <- arrow(
  angle = 20,
  ends = "first",
  type = "closed",
  length = grid::unit(8, "pt")
)
```

```{r}
pca_loadings |>
  filter(
    PC %in% c(1, 2)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = PC,
    names_prefix = "PC",
    values_from = value
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = PC1,
      y = PC2
    )
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      xend = 0,
      yend = 0
    ),
    arrow = arrow_style
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(
      label = column
    ),
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title = "Variable Loadings on PC1 and PC2",
    x = "PC1 loading",
    y = "PC2 loading"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Variance Explained by the Principal Components

The proportion of total variance explained by each principal component was extracted to assess how much information is retained by the first components.

```{r}
pca_variance <- pca_fit |>
  tidy(
    matrix = "eigenvalues"
  )

pca_variance
```

```{r}
pca_variance |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = PC,
      y = percent
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#56B4E9",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:10
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0, 0.01)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Variance Explained by Each Principal Component",
    x = "Principal component",
    y = "Variance explained"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

PC1 explained 31.9% of the total variance, while PC2 explained 20.4%. Together, the first two principal components explained 52.3% of the total variance in the selected variables.

## Cumulative Variance Explained

The first two principal components explain 52.3% of the total variance. However, this means that almost half of the information is not represented in the first two components. To better understand how much information we keep when adding more components, we can look at the cumulative variance explained.

```{r}
pca_variance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = cumulative)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = pca_variance$PC
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Variance Explained",
    x = "Number of principal components",
    y = "Cumulative variance explained"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This plot shows how the explained variance increases when more principal components are included. The dashed line marks 80% of the total variance, making it easier to see how many components are needed to reach this level. This helps us understand how much information can be retained while reducing the number of variables.

## Conclusion

Search for sexual dimorphism: No evidence of sexual dimorphism was found in the joint effect of age and BMI on diabetes (likelihood ratio test, p = 0.63), and the age × BMI interaction was not significant in either females or males. Diabetes probability increased with age and BMI in both sexes, but the differences between sexes observed in the plots were not statistically supported.

The cumulative variance plot shows that the first four components explain around 77% of the total variance, while five components explain more than 80%. This means that the first two components are useful for visualizing the data, but they do not capture all its variability. Including more components allows us to retain more information from the original dataset.
